items.title: 1.11 Applications of Exponential and Logarithmic Functions in Real-Life Situations

source_refs.note: Book p. 28-32: 1.11 intro; (i) growth and decay, Examples 22-23; (ii) decibels, Examples 24-26; (iii) discrete and continuous compound interest, Examples 27-28

blocks.text: Although there are many real-life situations involving exponential and logarithmic functions, in this section we focus on selected applications such as growth and decay processes, the measurement of sound intensity in decibels, and compound interest. Exponential models are used to describe quantities that change over time, while logarithmic functions help in determining unknown quantities in such models. The formula for growth and decay will be used as a given model and will be derived later in the chapter on differential equations, while the formulas for sound intensity and compound interest will be taken as standard results and will not be derived here.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Every problem on this page has the same shape: a formula (the model) links a quantity with time or with intensity.
If the unknown is the quantity itself, we only substitute and calculate.
If the unknown sits in the exponent (the time \(t\) or the constant \(k\)), we first make the exponential term stand alone and then take a logarithm of both sides. The logarithm brings the exponent down:
\[\ln(e^{x}) = x\]
\[\log(10^{x}) = x\]
\[\ln(a^{t}) = t\ln a\]
Use \(\ln\) when the base is \(e\), and \(\log\) (base 10) when the base is 10.
(i) Growth and Decay

Many natural and physical processes such as population growth and radioactive decay change in such a way that the rate of change is proportional to the current amount. These processes are known as exponential growth or decay.
The general mathematical model is:

blocks.text_alt: N equals N nought times e to the power k t

blocks.text: Where \(N_0\) is the initial amount, \(N\) is the amount at time \(t\), and \(k\) is a constant which is positive for growth and negative for decay.
In growth, the quantity increases with time, while in decay it decreases with time. Logarithms are used to determine unknown quantities such as time or rate in these models.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is \(N_0\) the initial amount? Put \(t = 0\): \(N = N_0e^{0} = N_0 \times 1 = N_0\).
Why does the sign of \(k\) decide growth or decay? If \(k > 0\), \(e^{kt}\) becomes larger as \(t\) increases. If \(k < 0\), \(e^{kt}\) becomes smaller and comes close to 0, but never reaches it.
'Rate of change proportional to the current amount' means: the more there is, the faster it changes. A bigger population has more births, so it grows faster; a bigger lump of radioactive material has more atoms breaking down each hour.
Method when \(t\) or \(k\) is unknown: (1) substitute the known values, (2) divide so that \(e^{(\dots)}\) stands alone, (3) take \(\ln\) of both sides, (4) solve the simple equation that is left.

blocks.title: Example 22
blocks.problem: A population is given by: \(N = 200e^{0.04t}\). Find the time \(t\) when the population becomes 400, where \(t\) is measured in hours. (Growth)
steps:
Given: \(N = 200e^{0.04t}\) and \(N = 400\).
To find: the time \(t\) (in hours).
Method: \(t\) is in the exponent, so substitute \(N = 400\), make \(e^{0.04t}\) stand alone, then take the natural logarithm, because the base is \(e\).

Substitute N = 400
\[400 = 200e^{0.04t}\]
Why: the model is true at every moment, including the moment the population is 400.

Make the exponential stand alone
\[\dfrac{400}{200} = e^{0.04t}\]
\[2 = e^{0.04t}\]
Why: dividing both sides by 200 leaves only \(e^{0.04t}\) on the right. We may not take \(\ln\) while 200 still multiplies it, because \(\ln(200e^{0.04t})\) is not \(0.04t\).

Take natural logarithm on both sides
\[\ln 2 = \ln(e^{0.04t})\]
\[\ln 2 = 0.04t\]
Why: \(\ln\) and \(e\) undo each other, \(\ln(e^{x}) = x\). This brings \(t\) down from the exponent.

Solve for \(t\)
\[t = \dfrac{\ln 2}{0.04}\]
\[= \dfrac{0.6931}{0.04}\]
\[\approx 17.33\]
Why: divide both sides by 0.04. The calculator gives \(\ln 2 \approx 0.6931\).

Check:
\[200e^{0.04 \times 17.33} = 200e^{0.6932}\]
\[\approx 200 \times 2.000 = 400\]
The population is 400, as required.
blocks.answer: Hence the population becomes 400 in about \(17.33\) hours.

blocks.title: Example 23
blocks.problem: A radioactive substance decays according to: \(N = 500e^{kt}\). After 20 hours, the amount becomes 300. Find the value of \(k\), where \(t\) is in hours. (Decay)
steps:
Given: \(N = 500e^{kt}\); \(N = 300\) when \(t = 20\).
To find: the constant \(k\).
Method: \(k\) is in the exponent. Substitute both known values, make \(e^{20k}\) stand alone, then take \(\ln\).

Substitute \(t = 20\) and \(N = 300\)
\[300 = 500e^{20k}\]
Why: the pair \(t = 20\), \(N = 300\) must satisfy the model.

Make the exponential stand alone
\[\dfrac{300}{500} = e^{20k}\]
\[\dfrac{3}{5} = e^{20k}\]
Why: divide both sides by 500 and reduce the fraction.

Take natural logarithm on both sides
\[\ln\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right) = 20k\]
Why: \(\ln(e^{20k}) = 20k\).

Solve for \(k\)
\[k = \dfrac{1}{20}\ln\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)\]
\[= \dfrac{-0.51083}{20}\]
\[\approx -0.02554\]
Why: divide by 20. \(\ln\frac{3}{5}\) is negative because \(\frac{3}{5} < 1\), so \(k\) comes out negative.

The book's rounded value
The book prints \(k \approx -0.0256\). Rounded to four decimal places, \(-0.025541\) is \(-0.0255\), because the fifth decimal digit is 4 (see the Book correction below).
Why: when the next digit is less than 5 we round down.

Check:
\[500e^{20 \times (-0.02554)} = 500e^{-0.5108}\]
\[\approx 500 \times 0.6000 = 300\]
The amount is 300 after 20 hours, and \(k < 0\) fits a decay.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Example 23: the book prints \(k \approx -0.0256\) (twice). The exact value is \(k = \frac{1}{20}\ln\frac{3}{5} = -0.025541\ldots\), which rounds to \(k \approx -0.0255\) at four decimal places. The method is correct; only the last digit of the rounding is off.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text:
Doubling time and half-life. A growth model doubles when \(e^{kt} = 2\), that is after \(t = \frac{\ln 2}{k}\), whatever the starting amount. In Example 22, \(\frac{\ln 2}{0.04} \approx 17.33\) hours: exactly the answer above, because 400 is double 200.
In the same way a decay model halves after \(t = \frac{\ln 2}{|k|}\) (the half-life).
(ii) Sound Intensity (Decibels)

The intensity of sound is the amount of sound energy passing through a unit area per unit time. Since sound intensity varies over a very wide range, it is measured on a logarithmic scale called the decibel (dB) scale.
The sound level \(L\) is given by:

blocks.text_alt: L equals 10 times log of I over I nought

blocks.text: where \(I\) is the intensity of sound and \(I_0\) is the threshold of hearing, which is the minimum sound intensity that a normal human ear can detect. Its standard value is given by:

blocks.text_alt: I nought equals 10 to the power minus 12 watts per square metre

blocks.text: where, \(\text{W/m}^{2}\) (watts per square meter) is the unit of sound intensity. It represents the amount of sound power (energy per second) passing through a unit area.

Because of the logarithmic scale, even a small increase in decibels represents a large change in actual sound intensity, which makes logarithmic laws very useful in comparing sound levels in real-life situations.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Here \(\log\) is the common logarithm (base 10), not \(\ln\).
Why a logarithmic scale? The intensities we can hear run from \(10^{-12}\) up to about \(1\ \text{W/m}^{2}\), a factor of a million million. The logarithm turns this huge range into the easy numbers 0 to 120 dB.
Two facts worth remembering: at the threshold \(I = I_0\), so \(L = 10\log 1 = 0\) dB; and every extra 10 dB multiplies the intensity by 10, because \(\frac{I}{I_0} = 10^{L/10}\).
To find \(I\) from \(L\): divide by 10, then change to exponential form, since \(\log x = y\) means \(x = 10^{y}\).

blocks.title: Example 24
blocks.problem: A sound has intensity \(I = 10^{-4}\) and reference intensity \(I_0 = 10^{-12}\). Find the sound level. (Finding sound level)
steps:
Given: \(I = 10^{-4}\), \(I_0 = 10^{-12}\) (both in \(\text{W/m}^{2}\)).
To find: the sound level \(L\) in dB.
Method: substitute directly into \(L = 10\log\left(\frac{I}{I_0}\right)\). The law of exponents \(\frac{10^{a}}{10^{b}} = 10^{a-b}\) simplifies the ratio, and \(\log(10^{x}) = x\) finishes it.

Substitute the values
The book prints: Substituting, \(I = 10^{-4}\) and \(I = 10^{-12}\). The second value is \(I_0\), the reference intensity (see the Book correction below).
\[L = 10\log\left(\dfrac{10^{-4}}{10^{-12}}\right)\]
Why: \(I\) goes on top and \(I_0\) underneath.

Simplify the ratio
\[\dfrac{10^{-4}}{10^{-12}} = 10^{-4-(-12)}\]
\[= 10^{8}\]
\[L = 10\log(10^{8})\]
Why: when dividing powers of the same base we subtract the exponents, and \(-4 + 12 = 8\).

Take the logarithm
\[L = 10 \times 8\]
\[= 80\ \text{dB}\]
Why: \(\log(10^{8}) = 8\), because \(\log\) has base 10.

Check:
\[10^{80/10} = 10^{8} = \dfrac{I}{I_0}\]
80 dB means the sound is \(10^{8}\) times the threshold, which matches \(10^{-4} \div 10^{-12}\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Example 24: the solution prints 'Substituting, \(I = 10^{-4}\) and \(I = 10^{-12}\)'. The second value is the reference intensity, so the line should read \(I = 10^{-4}\) and \(I_0 = 10^{-12}\). The working and the answer 80 dB are correct.

blocks.title: Example 25
blocks.problem: A sound has level \(L = 60\) dB and \(I_0 = 10^{-12}\). Find the intensity \(I\).
steps:
Given: \(L = 60\) dB, \(I_0 = 10^{-12}\ \text{W/m}^{2}\).
To find: the intensity \(I\).
Method: now the unknown is inside the logarithm. Substitute, divide by 10, then change the logarithmic form to exponential form.

Substitute into the formula
\[60 = 10\log\left(\dfrac{I}{10^{-12}}\right)\]
Why: \(L = 10\log\left(\frac{I}{I_0}\right)\) with the known values put in.

Divide both sides by 10
\[6 = \log\left(\dfrac{I}{10^{-12}}\right)\]
Why: the logarithm must stand alone before we change the form.

Convert to exponential form
\[10^{6} = \dfrac{I}{10^{-12}}\]
Why: \(\log x = y\) means \(x = 10^{y}\) (base 10).

Solve for \(I\)
\[I = 10^{6} \times 10^{-12}\]
\[= 10^{-6}\ \text{W/m}^{2}\]
Why: multiply both sides by \(10^{-12}\); when multiplying powers we add the exponents: \(6 + (-12) = -6\).

blocks.title: Example 26
blocks.problem: The sound levels at two points are \(L_1 = 90\) dB and \(L_2 = 60\) dB. Find the ratio of their intensities \(\frac{I_1}{I_2}\), where \(I_0 = 10^{-12}\ \text{W/m}^2\).
steps:
Given: \(L_1 = 90\) dB, \(L_2 = 60\) dB, \(I_0 = 10^{-12}\ \text{W/m}^{2}\).
To find: the ratio \(\frac{I_1}{I_2}\).
Method: write the decibel formula for each sound, change both to exponential form, then divide; \(I_0\) cancels.

Formula for the first sound
\[90 = 10\log\left(\dfrac{I_1}{I_0}\right)\]
\[9 = \log\left(\dfrac{I_1}{I_0}\right)\]
Why: substitute and divide by 10.

Formula for the second sound
\[60 = 10\log\left(\dfrac{I_2}{I_0}\right)\]
\[6 = \log\left(\dfrac{I_2}{I_0}\right)\]
Why: the same steps for the second level.

Converting in exponential form
\[\dfrac{I_1}{I_0} = 10^{9}\]
\[\dfrac{I_2}{I_0} = 10^{6}\]
Why: \(\log x = y\) means \(x = 10^{y}\).

Divide the two equations
\[\dfrac{I_1}{I_2} = \dfrac{10^{9}}{10^{6}}\]
\[= 10^{3} = 1000\]
Why: \(\frac{I_1/I_0}{I_2/I_0} = \frac{I_1}{I_2}\), so \(I_0\) cancels. We subtract exponents: \(9 - 6 = 3\).

Check:
The levels differ by 30 dB, that is three steps of 10 dB, and each step multiplies the intensity by 10: \(10 \times 10 \times 10 = 1000\).
blocks.answer: \(\frac{I_1}{I_2} = 10^{3} = 1000\), the required ratio of the intensities: the first sound is 1000 times as intense as the second.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A shortcut for comparing two sounds: subtracting the two formulas gives
\[L_1 - L_2 = 10\log\left(\dfrac{I_1}{I_2}\right)\]
In Example 26: \(30 = 10\log\frac{I_1}{I_2}\), so \(\frac{I_1}{I_2} = 10^{3}\). The value of \(I_0\) is never needed for a ratio.
(iii) Compound Interest

Compound interest is a method of calculating interest in which the interest earned in each period is added to the principal (initial amount), so that interest is earned on both the principal and the accumulated interest. This results in exponential growth of money over time and is widely used in banking and financial systems to model investment growth. Compound interest is generally classified into two types: discrete compounding and continuous compounding.
Discrete Compound Interest

Discrete compound interest is a method of calculating interest in which the interest is added to the principal at fixed time intervals such as yearly, half-yearly, quarterly, or monthly. In this method, interest is not added continuously, but only at specific intervals, and the future amount is calculated using a fixed compounding frequency. This type of compounding leads to exponential growth of money over time and is commonly used in banking systems.
The discrete compound interest is given by the formula:

blocks.text_alt: A equals P times open bracket 1 plus r over n close bracket to the power n t

items: \(r\) = Interest rate per unit time (in decimal form)
\(n\) = Number of times interest is compounded per unit time
\(t\) = Time (measured in the same unit as the compounding period)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Where does the formula come from? In each compounding period the rate is \(\frac{r}{n}\), so the money is multiplied by \(1 + \frac{r}{n}\). In \(t\) years there are \(nt\) periods, so we multiply \(nt\) times.
Small example: Rs. 1000 at 10% compounded annually becomes \(1000 \times 1.1 = 1100\) after one year and \(1100 \times 1.1 = 1210\) after two years, which is \(1000(1.1)^{2}\).
Values of \(n\): annually 1, half-yearly 2, quarterly 4, monthly 12.
Always write the rate as a decimal: \(8\% = 0.08\).
If the time \(t\) is unknown, take a logarithm of both sides and use \(\ln(a^{t}) = t\ln a\).
Continuous Compound Interest

Continuous compound interest is a method of calculating interest in which the interest is assumed to be added to the principal continuously at every instant of time. In this case, the compounding occurs without any fixed intervals, and the amount increases smoothly over time. This type of compounding represents the limiting case of discrete compounding when the number of compounding periods becomes infinitely large.
The formula for continuous compounding is:

blocks.text_alt: A equals P times e to the power r t

items: where, \(A\) = Final amount after time \(t\) (principal + interest)
\(r\) = Rate of interest per unit time (in decimal form)
\(t\) = Time (measured in the same unit as the rate is based on, such as years or months)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
'Limiting case' means: compound more and more often (\(n\) larger and larger) and the amount \(P\left(1 + \frac{r}{n}\right)^{nt}\) settles down to \(Pe^{rt}\). The table below shows this for Rs. 1000 at 5% per year for 3 years: the amounts increase, but only a little, and stop at \(1000e^{0.15}\).
Continuous compounding always gives slightly more than any discrete compounding at the same rate.

blocks.caption: Teaching table (ours): Rs. 1000 at 5% per year for 3 years

blocks.title: Example 27
blocks.problem: A sum of Rs. 1000 is invested at a rate of 5% per year compounded continuously for 3 years. Find the final amount.
steps:
Given: \(P = 1000\), \(r = 5\% = 0.05\), \(t = 3\).
To find: the final amount \(A\).
Method: the money is compounded continuously, so use \(A = Pe^{rt}\).

Formula for the continuous compound interest
\[A = Pe^{rt}\]
Why: 'compounded continuously' is the signal for this formula.

Substituting the values
\[A = 1000e^{0.05 \times 3}\]
\[A = 1000e^{0.15}\]
Why: \(rt = 0.05 \times 3 = 0.15\); the rate is used as a decimal.

Evaluate
\[e^{0.15} \approx 1.1618\]
\[A \approx 1000 \times 1.1618\]
\[= 1161.8\]
Why: the calculator gives \(e^{0.15} = 1.16183\ldots\)

Check:
Compounded annually the amount would be \(1000(1.05)^{3} = 1157.63\). Continuous compounding gives a little more, as it should (see the table above).
blocks.answer: Hence, the final amount after 3 years is \(A \approx\) Rs. 1161.8.

blocks.title: Example 28
blocks.problem: A sum of Rs. 5000 is invested at a rate of 8% per annum, compounded quarterly. Find the amount after 3 years.
steps:
Given: \(P = 5000\), \(r = 0.08\) (8% per annum), quarterly compounding \(n = 4\), \(t = 3\) years.
To find: the amount \(A\) after 3 years.
Method: interest is added at fixed intervals (every quarter), so use the discrete formula \(A = P\left(1 + \frac{r}{n}\right)^{nt}\).

Formula for the discrete compound interest
\[A = P\left(1 + \dfrac{r}{n}\right)^{nt}\]
Why: 'compounded quarterly' means four fixed additions per year.

Substituting the values
\[A = 5000\left(1 + \dfrac{0.08}{4}\right)^{4 \times 3}\]
\[A = (5000)(1.02)^{12}\]
Why: the rate per quarter is \(\frac{0.08}{4} = 0.02\), and 3 years have \(4 \times 3 = 12\) quarters.

Evaluate
\[(1.02)^{12} \approx 1.268242\]
\[A \approx 5000 \times 1.268242\]
\[\approx 6341.2\]
Why: use the power key of the calculator; round only at the end.

Check:
Compounded annually the amount would be \(5000(1.08)^{3} = 6298.56\). Quarterly compounding gives a little more, as expected.
blocks.answer: Hence, the amount after 3 years is \(A \approx\) Rs. 6341.2.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Growth and decay: \(N = N_0e^{kt}\); \(k > 0\) for growth, \(k < 0\) for decay; \(N_0\) is the amount at \(t = 0\).
2. When \(t\) or \(k\) is unknown: make the exponential stand alone, then take \(\ln\) of both sides.
3. Sound level: \(L = 10\log\left(\frac{I}{I_0}\right)\) with base-10 log and \(I_0 = 10^{-12}\ \text{W/m}^{2}\); every 10 dB multiplies the intensity by 10.
4. Discrete compounding: \(A = P\left(1 + \frac{r}{n}\right)^{nt}\); continuous compounding: \(A = Pe^{rt}\).
5. Rates always as decimals: \(5\% = 0.05\).
6. Check every answer by putting it back into the model.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Taking \(\ln\) before dividing: \(\ln(200e^{0.04t})\) is \(\ln 200 + 0.04t\), not \(0.04t\).
2. Using \(\ln\) in the decibel formula: it is \(\log\) to base 10.
3. Writing 8% as 8 instead of 0.08.
4. Forgetting \(n\) in the exponent: quarterly for 3 years is \(nt = 12\) periods at \(\frac{0.08}{4} = 0.02\) each.
5. Losing the minus sign of \(\ln\) of a number less than 1, which gives a negative time.
6. Rounding too early: keep four or more decimals until the last line.
